1.say: Read me your first sentence. 'That the price of bread has risen twice since March in every district of the region is clear.' By the time I reach 'is clear' I have forgotten what is clear. 'It is clear that the price of bread has risen twice since March, in every district of the region.' Short at the front, heavy at the back. The reader can hold it now. The next paragraph starts with inflation and ends with the bakery. And the paragraph before it ended with the bakery? No. It ended with wages. Then start this one with wages. Known first, new last, and the reader walks instead of jumping. 'Wages have not moved since January. Inflation, meanwhile, has taken nine per cent of them.' Better. Now the last line of the section. 'A subsidy on flour, which the ministry withdrew in April and has not restored, is the reason.' Same fault as the first sentence. Put the reason at the end, where its weight belongs. 'The reason is a subsidy on flour, withdrawn in April and never restored.'

grammar.label: end-weight — the heavy element goes last
grammar.meaning: English puts the long, new and complex part at the end

explanation.en: 'She sent to the committee the report she had spent a month on' is grammatical but hard; 'She sent the committee the report she had spent a month on' is easier because the heaviest phrase ends the sentence. Extraposition with 'it' is the same principle.
explanation.uz: Ingliz tilida eng uzun va yangi bo'lak gap oxirida turadi. 'it' bilan tuzilgan qurilmalar ham shu tamoyilga asoslanadi.

grammar.positive_example: It surprised everyone that the older method proved faster.
grammar.negative_example: That the older method proved faster surprised everyone.

l1_notes.uz: O'zbek tilida og'ir bo'lak boshda kelishi mumkin; ingliz tilida esa oxirida turgani o'qishni osonlashtiradi.

grammar.label: given before new — ordering information across sentences
grammar.form: known information first, new information last
grammar.meaning: each sentence starts from what the reader already has

explanation.en: A paragraph reads smoothly when each sentence opens with something the last one ended on. The passive exists partly for this: 'The committee rejected the plan. The plan had been written in a week' flows better as '…It had been written in a week.'
explanation.uz: Har bir gap oldingi gap tugagan narsadan boshlansa, matn silliq o'qiladi. Majhul nisbat qisman shu maqsadda mavjud.

grammar.positive_example: The committee rejected the plan. It had been written in a week.
grammar.negative_example: The committee rejected the plan. Somebody wrote it in a week, which was the plan.

l1_notes.uz: O'zbek tilida ma'lum-noma'lum tartibi so'z tartibi bilan beriladi; ingliz tilida esa nisbat tanlovi ham shu vazifani bajaradi.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: 'That the price of bread has risen twice since March in every district of the region is clear.'

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: By the time I reach 'is clear' I have forgotten what is clear.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: 'It is clear that the price of bread has risen twice since March, in every district of the region.'

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Short at the front, heavy at the back. The reader can hold it now.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: The next paragraph starts with inflation and ends with the bakery.

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: And the paragraph before it ended with the bakery?

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Then start this one with wages. Known first, new last, and the reader walks instead of jumping.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: 'Wages have not moved since January. Inflation, meanwhile, has taken nine per cent of them.'

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Better. Now the last line of the section.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: 'A subsidy on flour, which the ministry withdrew in April and has not restored, is the reason.'

body.speaker: Sarah
body.text: Same fault as the first sentence. Put the reason at the end, where its weight belongs.

body.speaker: Aziz
body.text: 'The reason is a subsidy on flour, withdrawn in April and never restored.'
